title: Self-Consuming Generative Models with Co-Evolving Human Preferences
claim: Model updates and user preferences form a coupled loop: curated outputs retrain the model while the model's outputs shift preferences.
layout: 2 stacked bands, left-to-right across time steps t and t+1, dashed divider
description: A wide two-band diagram split by a dashed vertical line into time steps t and t+1. The top light-blue band, 'Model & Data', runs left to right. A model icon feeds K sampled cat images, which go through Luce-choice curation to a single image. The curated set is mixed with a reference dataset of cat photos in a darker blue box, weighted (1-η) and η, to give the mixed dataset D_t. This trains the next model, which repeats the sample and curate steps and continues with an ellipsis. The bottom beige band, 'User Preference', shows horizontal bar charts over attributes such as softness and warmth. Blue bars show the current preference w_t and orange bars show the feature mean of the updated model. Vertical arrows link the bands: the preference reward r_t goes up to curation, and the observed feature mean goes down to update the preference. Formulas are written along the bottom band.
caption: Overview of the coupled model-user dynamics. Top row (model update): the current model pt generates K candidates, of which one is retained via preference-guided K-way Luce choice; the curated set Dcur is mixed with a reference dataset Dref at rate η to form Dt, on which pt+1 is trained. Bottom row (preference update): the user assesses how each candidate aligns with the current preference wt via the reward rt(x) = ⟨wt, φ(x)⟩, where φ is the feature map, and the preference vector then drifts toward the mean feature direction ¯φ(pt+1) of the updated model.
abstract: Generative models are increasingly trained in self-consuming iterative loops, where users curate preferred samples from model-generated candidates and the curated samples are used to train future generations of the model. Prior work has largely assumed fixed user preferences, but in practice exposure to model outputs gradually reshapes what users perceive as desirable, creating a feedback loop in which model distributions and user preferences co-evolve. We take a first step toward understanding the long-term behavior of such coupled dynamics. We show that when training relies entirely on user-curated synthetic data, iterative curation amplifies initial biases and drives the system toward one of multiple singleton equilibria in which the instance holding an initial advantage eventually dominates. In contrast, injecting reference data into training at a sufficiently large rate fundamentally changes the dynamics and yields a unique globally attracting equilibrium. Building on this insight, we study how reference-data injection can be used to control long-term outcomes, and propose an efficient algorithm that jointly selects a reference distribution and its mixing weight to steer the coupled system toward equilibria that preserve desired attributes while minimizing data collection costs.
